q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain:
x: Avogadro's law is about the number of molecules (moles). Equal numbers of atoms is wrong because molecules such as He, O₂ and O₃ have different numbers of atoms; masses and densities depend on the molar mass.

q: A gas occupies 400 cm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm. What volume will it occupy at 177 °C and 2 atm?
x: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 400 × (1/2) × (450/300) = 300 cm³. Ignoring the temperature gives 200 cm³, and using °C instead of K (177/27) gives about 1311 cm³.

q: Hydrogen is collected over water at 25 °C when the total pressure is 760 mm Hg. The vapour pressure of water at 25 °C is 24 mm Hg. The pressure of the dry hydrogen is:
x: By Dalton's law, P(total) = P(H₂) + P(water vapour), so P(H₂) = 760 − 24 = 736 mm Hg. Adding the vapour pressure instead of subtracting it gives 784 mm Hg.

q: Cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia solution is put at one end of a long glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other. A white ring of NH₄Cl forms:
o: Nearer the HCl end, because NH₃ is lighter and diffuses faster
Nearer the NH₃ end, because NH₃ is lighter and diffuses faster
Exactly in the middle, because both gases diffuse at the same rate
Nearer the HCl end, because HCl is heavier and diffuses faster
x: By Graham's law rate ∝ 1/√M; NH₃ (17) is lighter than HCl (36.5), so it travels further and the gases meet nearer the HCl end. Placing the ring near the faster gas's own end is the usual slip.

q: A sealed steel cylinder of gas is at 2.0 atm at 27 °C. If it is warmed to 57 °C, its pressure becomes:
x: At constant volume, P ∝ T (in K): P₂ = 2.0 × 330/300 = 2.2 atm. Using °C (2.0 × 57/27) gives about 4.2 atm; inverting the ratio gives 1.8 atm.

q: A 2 dm³ bulb of nitrogen at 3 atm is connected to a 3 dm³ bulb of oxygen at 2 atm, at the same temperature. After the gases mix, the total pressure is:
x: By Boyle's law each gas spreads into 5 dm³: p(N₂) = 3 × 2/5 = 1.2 atm and p(O₂) = 2 × 3/5 = 1.2 atm. By Dalton's law the total is 2.4 atm. Adding the starting pressures gives 5.0 atm, averaging them gives 2.5 atm, and 1.2 atm is only one partial pressure.

q: The gas constant R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In SI units its value is:
x: 1 dm³ atm = 101.3 J, so 0.0821 × 101.3 ≈ 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 1.987 is the value in cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 62.4 is in dm³ mm Hg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, not joules.

q: A 24.63 dm³ cylinder at 27 °C contains oxygen at a pressure of 5 atm. The mass of oxygen in the cylinder is: (O = 16; R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 300 = 24.63)
x: n = PV/RT = 5 × 24.63/24.63 = 5 mol; mass = 5 × 32 = 160 g. Taking the molar mass of oxygen as 16 g mol⁻¹ (atoms, not O₂) gives 80 g.

q: At what temperature will 2 mol of an ideal gas in a 16.42 dm³ vessel exert a pressure of 3 atm? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: T = PV/nR = (3 × 16.42)/(2 × 0.0821) = 300 K = 27 °C. Forgetting n = 2 gives 600 K (327 °C); leaving 300 as °C or adding 273 the wrong way gives the other values.

q: How many gas molecules are present in 1 cm³ of an ideal gas at STP? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: 22.4 dm³ = 22 400 cm³ holds 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, so 1 cm³ holds 6.02 × 10²³/22 400 = 2.69 × 10¹⁹. 2.69 × 10²² is the number per dm³ (cm³ not converted).

q: Equal masses of H₂ and O₂ are placed in two separate flasks of equal volume at the same temperature. The ratio of pressures, P(H₂) : P(O₂), is: (H = 1, O = 16)
x: At the same V and T, P ∝ n. For equal masses m, n(H₂) : n(O₂) = m/2 : m/32 = 16 : 1. 4 : 1 uses the square root as in Graham's law, and 1 : 16 inverts the ratio.

q: A 4.1 dm³ flask at 27 °C contains 0.8 g of helium and 3.2 g of oxygen. The total pressure in the flask is about: (He = 4, O = 16; R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 300 = 24.63)
x: n(He) = 0.8/4 = 0.2 mol and n(O₂) = 3.2/32 = 0.1 mol; total 0.3 mol. P = nRT/V = 0.3 × 24.63/4.1 ≈ 1.8 atm. Helium alone gives 1.2 atm, oxygen alone 0.6 atm, and treating oxygen as atoms (0.2 mol) gives 2.4 atm.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the actual volume of the gas molecules themselves, compared with the volume of the container, is:
x: The theory treats gas molecules as points whose own volume is negligible compared with the space they move in; this is one of the two postulates that fail for real gases at high pressure.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, when a gas is heated at constant pressure its volume increases because the molecules:
o: Become larger in size when heated
Attract each other more strongly at higher temperature
Move faster and strike the walls harder and more often, so the gas expands until the pressure falls back to its old value
Collide less often with the walls, because they move more slowly
x: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy, so collisions become harder and more frequent; at constant pressure the gas expands until the collision rate per unit area falls back. The molecules themselves do not grow.

q: At what temperature will oxygen molecules have the same root-mean-square speed as hydrogen molecules at 27 °C? (H = 1, O = 16)
x: c(rms) = √(3RT/M), so equal speeds need equal T/M: T/32 = 300/2, so T = 4800 K. Using the square-root ratio (×4) gives 1200 K, and dividing instead of multiplying gives 18.75 K.

q: The kinetic gas equation is PV = ⅓mNc̄². Since the total translational kinetic energy of the molecules is ½mNc̄², PV is equal to:
o: One-third of the total kinetic energy
Three-halves of the total kinetic energy
Two-thirds of the total kinetic energy
x: PV = ⅓mNc̄² = ⅔ × (½mNc̄²) = ⅔ × total kinetic energy. Taking the ⅓ directly as the fraction is the usual slip; (3/2) is the inverse relation, KE = (3/2)PV.

q: A fixed amount of an ideal gas has both its pressure and its volume doubled. The average kinetic energy of its molecules:
x: PV = nRT, so doubling both P and V makes PV, and hence T, four times larger. Average kinetic energy ∝ T, so it becomes four times as large. Thinking the two changes cancel gives 'stays the same'.

q: In a vessel at room temperature, gas molecules do not settle at the bottom under gravity. According to the kinetic molecular theory, this is because:
o: They are in rapid random motion and their kinetic energy is very large compared with the effect of gravity on them
The walls of the vessel attract them
x: Gas molecules move very fast in random directions and keep colliding, so gravity has only a tiny effect over the height of a vessel. Strong repulsion is not a postulate, and molecules do have mass.

q: In the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, the units of the constant a are:
x: an²/V² must have units of pressure, so a = P × V²/n² = atm dm⁶ mol⁻². dm³ mol⁻¹ is the unit of b, the volume correction.

q: At very high pressures, the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT of a real gas becomes greater than 1. This is because:
o: Attractive forces between the molecules become dominant
The molecules move faster at high pressure
The volume of the molecules themselves becomes significant, so the gas is harder to compress than an ideal gas
x: When the molecules are crowded together, their own volume is no longer negligible, so the real volume is larger than the ideal value and Z > 1. Dominant attractions would make Z less than 1, the opposite effect.

q: At 0 °C, hydrogen and helium show Z = PV/nRT greater than 1 at all pressures. The reason is that:
o: Their intermolecular attractions are very weak, so the effect of molecular volume dominates
x: H₂ and He are small, non-polar and hardly polarisable, so attractions (which lower Z) are tiny, and the excluded volume (which raises Z) wins. They are among the hardest gases to liquefy.

q: The critical temperature of a gas is:
o: The temperature at which the gas boils at 1 atm
The temperature above which the gas cannot be liquefied, however much pressure is applied
The temperature at which the gas becomes a plasma
The temperature at which its volume becomes zero
x: Above the critical temperature the molecules have too much kinetic energy for attractions to hold them as a liquid, so pressure alone cannot liquefy the gas. The boiling point at 1 atm is a lower, different temperature.

q: For a gas, the van der Waals constant a = 4.0 atm dm⁶ mol⁻². For 2 mol of this gas in a 4 dm³ vessel, the pressure correction term an²/V² is:
x: an²/V² = 4.0 × 2²/4² = 4.0 × 4/16 = 1.0 atm. Forgetting to square n and V (4.0 × 2/4) gives 2.0 atm.

q: 1 mol of a gas at 273 K and 100 atm occupies 0.20 dm³. Its compressibility factor and the main cause of its deviation are: (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; 0.0821 × 273 = 22.4)
o: Z ≈ 1.12; the volume of the molecules dominates
Z ≈ 0.89; attractive forces between molecules dominate
Z ≈ 0.89; the volume of the molecules dominates
Z ≈ 1.12; attractive forces between molecules dominate
x: Z = PV/nRT = 100 × 0.20/22.4 = 20/22.4 ≈ 0.89. Z < 1 means the gas is more compressible than ideal, which is due to attractions. Inverting the fraction gives 1.12; Z < 1 linked to molecular volume reverses the cause.
